extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, astronomers, surgeons, and physicians (readers/practitioners of the Philosophical Transactions, late 17th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical observational methodology for detecting the annual parallax of fixed stars: guidance on choice of stars, timing (solstices/tropics), instrument setup (fixed telescope + micrometer), and measurement strategy (azimuth and inter-star distance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-incisional extraction of bladder stones in females
rubrics_metrics.description: The stone may be extracted entire, or without incision, by dilating the urethra (using a speculum/dilating instrument) and employing a director and forceps to bring the stone away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patient positioning and restraint (child sitting across a table in a man's lap, arms tied down by a bandage) is used; operation can be rapid (about 3–4 minutes from first instrument) and with little pain; suitable for very young children and those of intermediate years and old age provided the stone is not immoderately large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty bladder before dilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pass a catheter into the neck of the bladder so it might empty itself of all urine before inserting the dilating instrument or speculum viscae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emptying the bladder prior to dilating reduces obstruction and allows safer extension of the urethra before extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dilating instrument/speculum viscae gently
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend the urethra as much as possible with safety, and without putting the patient to extraordinary pain, prior to extracting the stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dilation should be as extensive as safety allows but performed gently to minimize pain and avoid injury; after dilation use a director and forceps to extract the stone without incision when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid section (incision) when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The stone, if it be not of an immoderate size, may be extracted by only dilating the neck of the bladder; females should not be persuaded to undergo the section on any account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer extraction by dilation for safety; this method shown effective even in very young patients and in intermediate/old age when size permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification features of tubera terrae (truffles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truffles observed are included in a studded bark or coat; the inward substance is of the consistence of the fleshy part in a young chestnut, of a paste colour, of a rank odour, and unsavoury, streaked with many white veins or threads; globose though unequal and chinky, with papillae and fibres issuing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonality: most tender in spring, but after showers and sultry weather they may be plentifully found in autumn; fibres issuing and seed-vessel-like papillae suggest possible plant sui generis; identification should note coat, internal texture, odour, veins, and any issuing fibres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized cause of earthquakes (volcanic/combustible matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tremblings of the earth proceed from the same incensed matter which, finding a way through mountains (e.g., Mongibello), breaks out in smoke and fire; this combustible matter seems to be nitre mixed with other minerals and sulphur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed eruptions and effects to deflagration experiments (e.g., making salt of tartar by deflagration) as an analog; recognize two kinds of eruptions (frequent lesser disturbances and rare very violent eruptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational reporting criteria for earthquakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should record dates and sequence of shocks, geographic distribution (valleys, cities, villages), specific damages to buildings (churches, palaces, hospitals, fortifications), casualties, and secondary phenomena (smoke, flames, roaring sea, cracks in earth, lightning, deluges of rain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide town-by-town accounts with counts of dead/wounded and descriptions of structural failures; note behavioral observations (animals startled, birds flying, sea rising) and temporal progression (initial shocks followed by more terrible general shocks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic methodology for bone structure observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bone is constituted of tubes/tubuli of several sorts/sizes; what appear as globules on a smooth cut may be the tops of tubes — breaking the bone reveals tubuli which can be categorized into multiple sizes and arranged in rings analogous to wood growth rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both smooth cutting and breaking to reveal structure; identify multiple concentric rings of tubuli and relate larger tubuli to augmentation of bone; compare bone tubuli with wood's ring structure to infer growth and nourishment mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for studying tree bark and animal skin vessel orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine vessel orientation in bark (some run upwards; others circularly around the trunk) and in animal skin/scales (scales composed of interwoven vessels with a clear central spot) to determine origin and nourishment processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare different species (e.g., birch and cherry with circular vessels vs ash and oak with upward vessels); inspect many specimens; hypothesize growth origin (from trunk vs root) based on vessel pattern and thickness changes with tree growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal times for parallax observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe when the sun or earth are in the tropics, or nearly so (around the solstices), because at those times will be the greatest difference in meridional altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan observations at the solstices or times when Earth's position maximizes the parallactic angle; repeat observations over the year to detect changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of stars for parallax measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose stars as near as may be to the pole of the ecliptic or circumpolar stars nearer to the pole of the equator than our zenith; prefer bright stars (first and second magnitude) which are likely nearer to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on stars near the plane of the ecliptic; prefer bright circumpolar stars or those with convenient nearby companions so relative distances can be measured with a micrometer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure azimuth (east/west) rather than rising/setting
rubrics_metrics.description: If the meridional altitude differs at different times, so will the utmost east and west azimuth — these may be better observed than rising or setting and are less obnoxious to refraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on measuring utmost azimuths (east/west) where refraction is less problematic than near the horizon; use azimuth change as the principal observable for parallax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument setup: fixed telescopic object-glass and distant eye-glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix a good telescopic object-glass on some tower, steeple, or other high edifice and, at a due distance near the ground, build some place to fix the eye-glass so as to answer that object-glass — effectively an instrument whose radius is very large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a large effective radius instrument for precise angular measures; beware atmospheric refraction near the horizon may limit practicability of horizon-based observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of micrometer and thread orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit a micrometer to the fixed telescope so as to have its threads perpendicular to the horizon, to avoid inconvenience from diversity of refraction (if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the micrometer and telescope firmly fixed and protected from disturbance; ensure the instrument is carefully preserved and not disordered between observations so measurements across years are comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-star (companion) measurement strategy (Alcor example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a bright star with a nearby small star (e.g., the shoulder of the Lesser Bear and Alcor, distant about 9'–10'') and measure the distance between them at different times of year; if the inter-star distance differs, that indicates differing parallaxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method can reveal both that there is a parallax and that fixed stars are at different distances; if one star's parallax is discernible and the other's not, their relative distance change is detectable with a micrometer without moving the instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument quality, protection, and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary instruments of observation might be insufficient; a competent telescope furnished with a micrometer, firmly fixed on a suitable edifice and defended from wind and weather, is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure the instrument so it will not be disturbed between observations; protect lenses and micrometer from weather; ensure mechanical stability to permit year-to-year comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicalities of observing and measurement scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright first/second magnitude stars may be observed even in the daytime if their position is known; if it is necessary to move the micrometer to measure a companion, that may be done on another night — the inter-star distance will not change materially over a night or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations for parallax can be carried out at night or daytime (for bright stars) provided positions are known; measurements that require slight instrument movement can be scheduled across nearby nights without compromising year-to-year comparison.
